title: How do I know what God wants me to do?
seoTitle: How Do I Know God's Will? Wisdom for Big Decisions
description: Stuck on a big decision and afraid of missing God's will? What Scripture actually promises, Proverbs 3:5-6 and Jeremiah 29:11 in context, and what to do.
summary: For anyone stuck at a fork and afraid of missing God's will: what he has already said, and how to choose well.
askedAs: how do I know God's will
what does God want me to do with my life
what if I missed God's will
answer: You're facing a decision, a job, a move, a person, maybe the direction of your whole life, and you've prayed and still don't know which way God wants you to go. Underneath it there's often a fear that God has one right answer hidden somewhere, and that if you miss it you'll spend your life outside his will. Scripture doesn't treat his will as a riddle. Most of what God wants he has already made clear, and it has more to do with who you're becoming than with which door you choose. For the rest, he promises wisdom to anyone who asks, never meant you to decide alone, and remains Lord of whatever road you take. Tonight, write the decision down in one sentence and pray it plainly. It doesn't have to be settled by morning.
happening:
It rarely feels like a theology question. It feels like lying awake at two in the morning, running two futures side by side until both blur. You make the list of pros and cons, then make it again. You ask three friends and get three answers. You pray, the ceiling stays quiet, and you start reading ordinary things as messages: the verse the Bible happened to fall open to, the delay that surely means something. Some people are stuck at one fork. Others are stuck on the biggest question there is, what God wants them to do with their one life, and feel as if everyone else got a calling while they got silence.

There are honest explanations for why this is so hard, and each gets something right. Part of it is the mind under pressure: when a choice feels permanent, it rehearses every outcome, and the fear of regret can freeze a person more than the choice itself. Part of it can be the body. When being unable to decide spreads to small things and comes with poor sleep or a heaviness that won't lift, a doctor should hear about it, because a worn-out body makes every fork look like a cliff. And part of it is spiritual. People will tell you to pray harder and watch for open and closed doors, and there's truth in that, because prayer matters and God does open and shut doors.

What they leave out is the assumption under the question: that God's will is mostly hidden information, and that missing it would leave you outside his will for good. That assumption turns prayer into code-breaking and every coincidence into a clue, and it can make a person strangely passive, waiting for certainty before obeying anything. In Micah 6 a worshiper asks what God wants and keeps raising the offer, calves, then thousands of rams, then rivers of oil, then his own firstborn. The answer comes back plain: "He has shown you, O man, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?" (Micah 6:8).

None of this makes your decision small. It puts it in its place. The choice in front of you matters to God, but it sits inside a will he has already revealed, and the choosing itself is one of the ways he makes a person wise.

scripture.intro: Two verses come up again and again when Christians face a decision, Proverbs 3:5-6 and Jeremiah 29:11, and both are usually read alone. Read in their settings, they carry more than the way we use them. Beside them stand two New Testament passages that say how God's will is known: by a mind he is renewing, and by asking him for wisdom he is glad to give.

passages.text: My son, do not forget my teaching, but let your heart keep my commandments; ... Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways acknowledge Him, and He will make your paths straight. Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD and turn away from evil.
passages.reading: Proverbs 3 is a father talking to his son, one of the talks in chapters 1 to 9 where an older man hands a younger one a way of life. Plenty of us never had a father sit us down like this. I didn't, and I don't take this voice for granted. "Lean not on your own understanding" can't mean *stop thinking*, because this same father tells his son to get understanding above everything (Proverbs 4:7). The warning is spelled out in verse 7: don't be wise in your own eyes. The word translated "acknowledge" is the ordinary Hebrew word for knowing, so the call is to know God in every corner of an ordinary day. And straight paths, in Proverbs, are a life kept upright and clear of ruin, a way of living rather than a route drawn in advance for every turn.

passages.text: This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says to all the exiles who were carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon: Build houses and settle down. Plant gardens and eat their produce. ... Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles. Pray to the LORD on its behalf, for if it prospers, you too will prosper. ... When Babylon’s seventy years are complete, I will attend to you and confirm My promise to restore you to this place. For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans to prosper you and not to harm you, to give you a future and a hope. Then you will call upon Me and come and pray to Me, and I will listen to you. You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart.
passages.reading: Jeremiah sent this letter to the exiles carried off to Babylon with King Jeconiah in 597 BC (Jeremiah 29:1-2). Others were promising them a quick return, and midway through the letter God warns them against diviners and the dreams they went looking for (29:8-9). His word was harder: build, plant, marry, pray for the city that conquered you, and settle in for seventy years. Many who first received the letter would not live to see the promise kept. The "you" in verse 11 is plural in Hebrew. The promise belongs to a people across generations, and that makes it sturdier than a personal guarantee: it stayed true for those who died in Babylon, because it never depended on how any one life turned out. And notice where the plans lead: to prayer, and to God himself, found by those who search for him with all their heart.

passages.text: Therefore I urge you, brothers, on account of God’s mercy, to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual service of worship. Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.
passages.reading: Paul wrote to the believers in Rome, a city he hadn't yet visited, after eleven chapters on the mercy of God, and his "therefore" carries all of it. Here God's will is something a changing mind learns to recognize, and "test and approve" describes a skill that grows. The means are ordinary and costly: your whole embodied life offered to God, and a refusal to let this age shape your thinking, including its insistence that every choice has to prove who you are. Paul was writing to a congregation, and the next verses turn straight to the body of Christ (Romans 12:4-5). The renewing happens among other believers, over years, until a person can look at two good options and see which one fits the life God is making.

passages.text: Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him. But he must ask in faith, without doubting, because he who doubts is like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind. That man should not expect to receive anything from the Lord. He is a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.
passages.reading: James wrote to believers scattered far from home (James 1:1), and he begins with trials (1:2-4), so the wisdom he promises is for people under pressure, which is where big decisions usually find us. God gives it generously and "without finding fault," so you don't have to apologize for asking again. The lines about doubt have frightened plenty of indecisive Christians, but the same word, double-minded, returns in chapter 4 for people trying to be friends with the world and with God at once (James 4:4, 8). The doubter James means has a divided heart, asking God for wisdom while keeping another master in reserve, ready to ignore the answer if it costs too much. The person who honestly doesn't know which road to take, and asks anyway, is doing exactly what James said to do.

whyHard:
For most of history, most people inherited much of what we now have to choose, from the work they did to the person they married. Nobody should be nostalgic for that world and its narrow freedom. But it means the fork that seems to hold your entire life is, for most people who ever lived, a new kind of weight.

The modern world opened those forks and then loaded them with meaning. The philosopher Charles Taylor traced an ideal that first took shape in the late eighteenth century: that each person has an original way of being human, and that a life which never finds its own way has missed the point. If that's true, every large choice becomes a verdict on whether you found yourself, and a job or a city stops being a place to serve and becomes a wager on who you are.

The church didn't so much resist this as translate it. Many of us learned to picture God's will as an individual blueprint, one right job and one right spouse chosen in advance and hidden until we find them, and phrases like *God's perfect will* and *God's second best* gave the fear a religious vocabulary. Those of us who preach have fed this, telling people to wait for a peace and watch for doors as if faith were a scavenger hunt. A skeptic sees superstition. I came to faith out of atheism, so I understand the suspicion, and the Bible shares it: Israel was forbidden to read omens (Deuteronomy 18:10).

Christians who believe God has a specific path for each life are holding on to something true: the God who numbers the hairs of your head led Abraham out of Haran and Paul across the sea to Macedonia. What our anxiety adds is the belief that his path is hidden from us, and that one wrong reading could ruin a life.

Notice what the secular story and the anxious religious one share. Both put the whole weight of a life on getting one choice right. Both make the self the only stage, so the question is always what God wants for me and never what he is doing with his people. And both turn the future into a test you could fail. What sounds like devotion is often our culture's fear, speaking in the Bible's words.

There's a harder thing to say, and it includes me. Wanting a sign can be humility, but it can also be a wish to be spared responsibility, since if God tells me exactly what to do, the outcome is his to answer for. Or it can be a wish for control, to see the ending before I agree to begin. Moses told Israel, "The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us and to our children forever, so that we may follow all the words of this law" (Deuteronomy 29:29). We reach for the secret things because the revealed ones ask more of us. Forgiving a brother, telling the truth at work, keeping a vow, loving the neighbor in front of you: none of it needs a sign, and all of it costs something.

The church has stood at this fork before, and it didn't get through with better signs. The apostles cast lots once, in Acts 1, before the Spirit was poured out; after Pentecost the New Testament never shows the church deciding that way again. When the young church faced the question that could have split it, whether Gentile believers had to keep the law of Moses, its leaders argued, listened, searched the Scriptures, and reached a judgment they described with striking modesty: "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us" (Acts 15:28). God was in it, and so were they. The will you're afraid of missing was never a map hidden in the sky. It is a people God is forming, and Jesus named its heart when he said the Father's will is that he "shall lose none of those He has given Me" (John 6:39).

thisWeek.intro: You don't have to settle this tonight. What you need is a way through it that's honest before God and fair to the people your choice will touch. These steps can take a week or two, and the first one takes five minutes.

steps.title: Write the decision in one sentence
steps.body: Get it out of your head and onto paper as plainly as you can: *Do I take the new job, or stay where I am?* Under it, write what you're afraid will happen if you choose wrong. Then pray both sentences, out loud if you can, and ask God for the wisdom he has promised. A decision often looks smaller once you can see its actual size.

steps.title: Get the real facts
steps.body: Fear feeds on vague information. Find out what each option actually involves: the pay and the hours, the cost of moving, what it means for your family, the deadline, what you'd give up. If the decision touches your health, the law, or serious money, get a qualified professional's view before you choose. God has always worked through people who know what we don't.

steps.title: Start with what God has already said
steps.body: Before you worry about God's hidden will, hold both options up to his revealed one. If either would require you to lie or to neglect someone who depends on you, it's off the table. Jesus summed up the law as loving God with all you are and your neighbor as yourself (Matthew 22:37-40), so ask which road would help you do both. Scripture usually narrows the field more than people expect.

steps.title: Ask two or three wise people
steps.body: Choose people who know you and know the Scriptures, and who gain nothing from what you decide. Give them the whole picture, including the part you're tempted to leave out, and ask what they see that you don't. "Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed" (Proverbs 15:22). You're not handing them the decision. You're letting the body of Christ do what it was made to do.

steps.title: Give it a few days and notice
steps.body: Keep praying for several days and notice what happens in you as you picture each road. Ignatius of Loyola, in the sixteenth century, taught people to watch for consolation, the movements that draw you toward God with more faith, hope, and love, and for desolation, which drags you toward darkness and restlessness, where God feels far away. He counseled never to reverse a decision in a time of desolation. So don't decide in a panic, and don't undo a clear decision in a dark week.

steps.title: Decide, then keep faith
steps.body: Set a date, make the decision, and tell someone you trust. Then stop re-deciding it every night. James teaches us to hold every plan humbly, saying, "If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that" (James 4:15), and that humility guards you from arrogance before the choice and from torment after it. A hard road doesn't prove you missed God. Hard roads run all through Scripture, and so does the God who walks them with his people.

moreHelp.body:
Most decisions need only prayer, Scripture, wise friends, and time. Some need more. If the indecision has spread into the rest of your life, if worry about it is costing you sleep or work, or you're afraid any choice will anger God and nothing quiets that fear for long, please see a doctor or a licensed counselor. That kind of fear deserves real care, and needing care is no failure of faith. If the decision itself involves your health, the law, or serious money, bring a doctor, a lawyer, or a qualified financial professional in before you choose. And if you're deciding whether to leave someone who frightens or hurts you, your safety comes first: call 911 if you're in danger, and use the confidential hotlines on [our Find Help page](/help#help-now).

To find a counselor, ask your doctor for a referral, search your insurance company's directory, or ask a pastor which local counselors they trust. If you want a Christian counselor, ask about that directly. Whoever you see, check that they're licensed in your state.
signs: You haven't been able to make even small decisions for weeks, and it's getting worse.
Worry about choosing wrong is keeping you from sleeping, eating, or working.
You're afraid any choice will anger God, and no reassurance helps for long.
The decision involves medical treatment, a legal matter, or serious debt.
You're deciding whether to leave someone who threatens, controls, or hurts you.
A leader insists God told them what you must do and treats disagreement as rebellion.
You've begun to think others would be better off without you. Call or text 988 tonight.
moreHelp.firstCall: You don't need a speech. You might say: *I've been stuck on a big decision for a while, and the worry is starting to affect my sleep and my work. I'd like help thinking clearly.* Ask whether they have openings, whether they take your insurance, and what a session costs. If your faith matters to you, say so, and ask how they work with Christian clients. With a lawyer or financial professional, name the decision and ask what you need to understand first.
moreHelp.cost: Cost shouldn't keep you from help. Many counselors offer sliding-scale fees based on income, and community mental health centers and university training clinics usually charge less. If you're employed, ask whether your employer has an employee assistance program, which often includes a few free sessions. Your church may have a benevolence fund for needs like this. For legal questions, legal aid organizations and your local bar association can point you toward low-cost help.

helping.body:
If someone you love is stuck, listen longer than feels comfortable. People usually know more than they think; they need room to say it out loud, and someone who will ask what they're afraid of. Help them separate the decision from the fear, and the facts from the guesses.

Be careful with your own authority. Anyone with standing in a person's life, a parent or a pastor especially, can become the voice they obey instead of the voice that helps them think. If you have something to gain or lose from their choice, say so plainly, never claim God told you what they should do, and leave them free to disagree. I'm raising five sons, and I'm convinced the aim of a parent's counsel is a grown child who can choose wisely when you're not in the room, which only happens if you let them choose. Pastors carry the same temptation with more weight. Our work is to help people hear Scripture and one another, not to become their conscience.
say: What are you most afraid will happen?
Walk me through an ordinary Tuesday on each road.
God isn't hiding the answer from you.
Whatever you decide, I'm not going anywhere.
Can I pray with you about it right now?
dontSay: God told me what you should do.
If you had more faith, you'd know.
You'll never get another chance like this.
Stop overthinking it and trust God.
helping.next: Offer to be one of their counselors for a set stretch of time, and help them choose a date to decide so the question doesn't hang open forever. Check in after they choose, especially if the road turns hard. If you see the signs listed above, help them reach a doctor or a counselor, and if they speak of ending their life, stay with them and call or text 988 together.

prayer:
Father, I don't know what to do. I've made the lists and asked the people and lain awake with it, and I'm tired of the sound of my own reasoning. When Jehoshaphat stood before an army too big for him, he prayed, "We do not know what to do, but our eyes are upon You." That's where I am.

Forgive me for wanting a sign when you've already told me so much, and for wanting to see the ending before I'll take a step. Give me the wisdom you promised to give without scolding, and friends who will tell me the truth. Make me someone who could walk either road and still love you on it.

Your Son knelt in the dark and asked for another way, and then he said yes to yours. I can't pray it the way he did, but I want to want your will more than I want certainty. If I'm about to walk into harm, stop me. And whatever I choose, don't let me mistake a hard road for your absence. Amen.

faq.q: Does God have a specific plan for my life?
faq.a: Christians answer this in more than one way, and the creeds don't settle it. Some believe God has a particular path for each person, made known through Scripture, prayer, circumstances, and the Spirit's leading, as when he called Abraham and sent Paul to Macedonia. Others believe God's plan is found within his revealed will: become like Christ, love your neighbor, and within those bounds choose wisely and freely, as Paul told a widow she was "free to marry anyone she wishes, as long as he belongs to the Lord" (1 Corinthians 7:39). Both agree that nothing in your life escapes God's knowledge and care, and both lead to much the same practice: pray, search the Scriptures, seek counsel, choose, and trust him.

faq.q: What if I make the wrong decision?
faq.a: Choices have real consequences, and some can't be undone. But Scripture never tells a believer that one wrong turn has put them beyond God's reach. When Joseph's brothers sold him, the worst decision in that family's history, he could later tell them, "what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good" (Genesis 50:20). If your choice involved sin, confess it and make what amends you can; God forgives. If you chose one good thing over another, you haven't lost his care. The God who met his people in Babylon can meet you on the road you took.

faq.q: Should I ask God for a sign?
faq.a: You can bring God your longing for a clear answer, and sometimes he gives one. But Scripture doesn't teach us to decide by signs. When Gideon laid out his fleece, God had already told him plainly what to do, and Gideon said as much (Judges 6:14, 36-37). God was patient with his fear, and the story never holds it up as a method. Psalm 32 promises instruction in the way we should go, then warns, "Do not be like the horse or mule, which have no understanding" (Psalm 32:9). God would rather guide a person who understands than steer an animal with a bit.

faq.q: How do I know if it's God or just me?
faq.a: Test it the way the church always has. Does it agree with what God has already said in Scripture? Does it look like Jesus, or does it flatter your pride or feed your fear? Do wise people who know you recognize it? Does it hold steady through days of prayer? God can speak to a person quietly, and Christians disagree about how often he does. But an impression that contradicts Scripture isn't from him, however strong it feels. Be slow to say *God told me*, especially when those words would end the conversation with people who love you.

faq.q: Should I wait until I have peace about it?
faq.a: Peace is a real gift, and a settled sense of God's nearness over time is worth noticing. But peace can't carry the whole decision. A lack of peace is sometimes only fear of a hard thing you should do anyway, and a feeling of peace is sometimes only relief at avoiding it. Jesus had no ease in Gethsemane, and he still prayed, "Yet not My will, but Yours be done" (Luke 22:42). The verse often quoted here, "Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts," continues, "for to this you were called as members of one body" (Colossians 3:15). It's about peace among believers, one more reason to decide with others.

slots.note: The page says only that James came to faith out of atheism and so understands the skeptic's suspicion of sign-seeking. He could add, in his own words, whether coming to faith as a former atheist shaped how he first thought about God's will; his essay How to Find God's Will for Your Career says the new convert in him turned a silent universe into one full of hidden signals. The section stands without it.

Where James lands on the in-house question in the first answer: whether God has an individual plan for each life that believers must discover, or guides mainly through his revealed will and the wisdom he gives. His career essay leans toward the second. The answer states both views fairly and names that the creeds do not settle it; if he wants his own landing here, it should be in his words.

The Proverbs 3 reading says only that James never had a father sit him down this way. He could add a sentence of his own about what the father-to-son voice of Proverbs 1 to 9 means to a man raised without a father.
The section states only James's conviction as a father of five sons. He could add, in his own words, how he counsels his sons through big decisions; no story has been written for him.

In Proverbs 3:6 the verb translated acknowledge is the Hebrew verb for knowing (da'ehu, from yada).

sources.claim: In Jeremiah 29:11 the pronoun you is plural in Hebrew (lakhem, aleikhem).

sources.claim: Charles Taylor traces to the late eighteenth century (Herder) the ideal that each person has an original way of being human, and that failing to live it is missing the point of one's life.

reviewed.notes: Writer's self-review, awaiting the editor. node scripts/validate-needs.mjs decisions runs clean. All four passages were copied from node scripts/bsb.mjs; the Jeremiah blockquote drops only the BSB's inner speech marks and marks its gaps with ellipses, and every double-quoted line in prose is verbatim BSB with its reference. Every kit link, the inline /help#help-now link, and each passage's Study Bible chapter resolve as live routes (none unverified, none redirected). The claim that the church never casts lots after Acts 1:26 was checked against the BSB text of Acts through Revelation. Non-Scripture facts are listed in sources; their pages could not be opened from the build environment, so each was confirmed through search-engine excerpts and should be opened once before release. No statistics, no quotations but Scripture, no invented stories or people. James's life appears only as stance (atheism, raised without a father, five sons), and slots mark where his own words belong. The in-house question of an individual will for each life is stated both ways without a landing. Read as the midnight reader (a first step inside the answer), the skeptic (the superstition charge conceded, and Scripture's own ban on omens), and the pastor (pastors implicated first, and a warning sign for a leader who claims to speak for God).
